why.q: Why is the sky blue?
why.a: Sunlight reaches Earth’s atmosphere and is scattered in all directions by the gases and particles in the air. Sunlight looks white, but it is actually a blend of all the rainbow colors. Blue light travels in shorter, smaller waves compared to red or yellow light.

why.q: Why does the Moon have craters?
why.a: The Moon is constantly hit by flying space rocks like asteroids and meteoroids. On Earth, our thick atmosphere acts as a shield, burning up most space rocks before they can touch the ground. The Moon has no protective atmosphere, so every space rock crashes straight into its surface, blasting out giant, bowl-shaped dents called craters.

why.q: Why are planets round?
why.a: Planets are round because of gravity, a powerful force that pulls everything toward an object's center. When a planet is forming, it gathers more and more space material. As it grows bigger and heavier, its gravity gets much stronger.

why.q: Why is space black if the Sun is so bright?
why.a: On Earth, the daytime sky is bright because our atmosphere is full of gas and tiny particles that scatter sunlight in every direction. Space is a vacuum, which means it is almost completely empty of matter. Because there is almost no air, gas, or dust in space to bounce and scatter the light from the Sun or other stars, the light travels in straight, invisible lines.

why.q: Why do stars twinkle but planets do not?
why.a: Stars twinkle because they are incredibly far away and appear as tiny, single points of light. As their light passes through Earth's atmosphere, it travels through shifting layers of warm and cool air that bend it back and forth, making the star look like it is blinking. Planets are much closer, so they look like tiny disks instead of points.

why.q: Why are some stars red and other stars blue?
why.a: Just like a flame on a stove, a star's color tells us exactly how hot it is! A star's temperature depends mostly on how big and heavy it is. Heavier stars squeeze their fuel harder and burn it faster, so they get much hotter.

why.q: Why is the Sun so incredibly hot?
why.a: The Sun is hot because it is a giant nuclear engine! Deep inside the Sun's core, the pressure and gravity are so intense that they squeeze hydrogen atoms together to make helium. This process is called nuclear fusion, and it releases a mind-blowing amount of energy.

why.q: Why does the Moon look like it is changing its shape every night?
why.a: The Moon does not actually change its shape, and it does not make its own light. What we call moonlight is actually just sunlight reflecting off the Moon's surface like a giant mirror. As the Moon travels in a circle around Earth, the Sun always lights up exactly half of it.

why.q: Why do we only ever see one side of the Moon from Earth?
why.a: We only see one side of the Moon because of a perfect cosmic dance called tidal locking! The Moon spins on its own axis at the exact same speed that it travels around the Earth. It takes the Moon about 27 days to spin around once, and also about 27 days to complete one loop around our planet.

why.q: Why do solar and lunar eclipses happen?
why.a: Eclipses happen when the Earth, Moon, and Sun line up in a straight line. In a solar eclipse, the Moon slides between the Sun and Earth. Its shadow falls on a narrow strip of Earth, and for a few minutes the sky goes dark like night.

why.q: Why do we have four different seasons on Earth?
why.a: Many people think we have seasons because Earth gets closer to the Sun, but that is actually a myth! We have seasons because Earth's axis—the imaginary pole running through its center—is tilted slightly to the side. As Earth travels around the Sun, different parts receive more direct sunlight.

why.q: Why is Venus hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer to the Sun?
why.a: Mercury is closest to the Sun, but it has almost no atmosphere to hold onto its heat, so it gets freezing cold at night. Venus is nearly twice as far from the Sun as Mercury, but it is wrapped in a super-thick, heavy atmosphere filled with carbon dioxide gas and yellow acid clouds. This thick layer acts like a giant greenhouse blanket, trapping the Sun's heat on the surface.

why.q: Why does Jupiter have a giant red spot that looks like an eye?
why.a: Jupiter's famous Great Red Spot is not a solid landmark. It is actually a colossal, wild storm that has been spinning for hundreds of years! Because Jupiter is a giant ball of gas with no solid ground to slow storms down, its storms can last for centuries.

why.q: Why do comets grow long, glowing tails when they get close to the Sun?
why.a: Comets are like giant, dirty snowballs made of ice, dust, and rock. When a comet comes close to the hot Sun, its surface ice warms up and turns straight into gas. This escaping gas and dust gets pushed away from the Sun by sunlight and the solar wind.

why.q: Why doesn't the Earth fall directly into the Sun?
why.a: The Sun's massive gravity is constantly pulling the Earth toward it, but the Earth is not falling in because it is moving sideways extremely fast, at about 67,000 miles per hour. Without gravity, Earth would zoom off in a straight line into deep space. Instead, the Sun's gravity keeps bending Earth's path.

why.q: Why do we see "shooting stars" streak across the night sky?
why.a: "Shooting stars" are not actually stars at all! They are tiny bits of space rock and dust, called meteoroids, that crash into Earth's atmosphere. Most are no bigger than a grain of sand, but they zoom in at tens of thousands of miles per hour.

why.q: Why do things on Earth fall down instead of floating away?
why.a: Everything falls down because of gravity, which is an invisible pulling force that all physical objects have. The strength of gravity depends on how heavy and massive an object is. Because the Earth is absolutely humongous compared to us, its gravitational pull is incredibly strong.

why.q: Why do rockets need massive engines and so much fire to blast off?
why.a: To break free from Earth's strong gravitational pull and reach space, a rocket must travel incredibly fast. Rockets use massive engines to burn giant tanks of fuel, creating hot gas that explodes downward out of the nozzle. According to a rule of science, every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

why.q: Why do astronauts have to wear heavy, puffy white spacesuits?
why.a: In space there is no air to breathe, it can be freezing cold or boiling hot, and there is harmful radiation from the Sun. A spacesuit is actually a wearable, one-person spaceship! It is white because white reflects the Sun's heat, which helps keep the astronaut from getting too hot.

why.q: Why do we send robotic rovers to explore Mars instead of humans?
why.a: Mars is a cold, dry desert with thin air that humans cannot breathe, and the journey takes many months. It is currently much safer and easier to send robotic rovers instead of people. Rovers do not need water, food, or oxygen to survive, and they do not get tired!

why.q: Why are flamingos pink?
why.a: Flamingos are not born pink. Chicks hatch covered in gray-white fluff. Their color comes from their food.

why.q: Why do cats purr?
why.a: Often a purring cat is happy and relaxed, but that is not the whole story. Cats also purr when they are nervous, hurt, hungry or sitting at the vet. Kittens purr to their mother when they are only days old, before they can see or hear.

why.q: Why do bats live in caves?
why.a: Not all bats do. Many roost in trees, under bridges or in attics. But caves suit bats beautifully.

why.q: Why do dogs wag their tails?
why.a: A wag means the dog is excited about something, and excited is not the same as friendly. A loose, sweeping wag with a wiggly body usually means a happy dog. A stiff, fast flick with the tail held high can mean a dog that may bite.

why.q: Why do dogs have wet noses?
why.a: A few reasons, and none of them is a health test. Glands inside a dog's nose make a thin layer of watery mucus. Smell chemicals in the air dissolve in that damp lining, and only once they are dissolved can the smelling cells inside the nose pick them up.

why.q: Why do pigs roll around in mud?
why.a: Pigs are not being dirty. They are cooling off. People sweat all over to lose heat, but a pig has very few working sweat glands, so sweating hardly helps at all.

why.q: Why do cows chew the cud?
why.a: Grass is tough stuff, and a cow cannot digest it alone. She swallows it fast into the rumen, the biggest of her stomach's four chambers, where trillions of tiny microbes soften it. Later, resting, she brings a lump back up.

why.q: Why do zebras have black and white stripes?
why.a: Zebras live where biting flies, like horseflies, spread nasty diseases. When flies zoom toward a zebra, the bold stripes seem to confuse them, so they bump into the animal or sail past instead of landing softly. Researchers even dressed plain horses in striped coats, and far fewer flies landed.

why.q: Why do giraffes have such long necks?
why.a: A giraffe's neck can be six feet long, yet it holds only seven bones, the same number as in your neck. Scientists still argue about why it got so long. One idea: long necks let giraffes reach leaves that shorter animals cannot, especially in dry seasons.

why.q: Why do kangaroos have pouches?
why.a: A baby kangaroo, called a joey, is born after only about a month, when it is no bigger than a jellybean and barely formed. It cannot survive on its own, so it crawls up through its mother's fur into her pouch, a fold of skin she can hold shut with muscles. Inside are the teats it drinks from.

why.q: Why do camels have humps?
why.a: Not water, fat. A camel's hump is a big store of fatty tissue, food the camel lives off when meals are scarce. Piling that fat into one lump instead of spreading it under the skin is clever: a full fat blanket would trap heat, and deserts get blazing hot.

why.q: Why do woodpeckers not get headaches?
why.a: For years people said a woodpecker's skull worked like a built-in cushion. High-speed videos in 2022 showed otherwise: the beak and head stop together, so the head is really a stiff hammer. What saves the bird is being small.

why.q: Why can hummingbirds hover in mid-air?
why.a: Most birds get nearly all their lift on the downstroke, so they must keep moving forward. A hummingbird sweeps its wings almost flat, forward and back rather than up and down, tracing a figure eight. At the end of each sweep it turns the wing right over, so it pushes air downward on the way back as well as on the way forward.

why.q: Why do honeybees do a waggle dance?
why.a: A honeybee that finds a good patch of flowers comes home and dances on the honeycomb. She runs in a straight line, wiggling her body, then loops back and repeats. Inside the dark hive she can feel which way is up.

why.q: Why do spiders spin webs?
why.a: A web is a hunting net that works while the spider rests. Spiders make silk inside their bodies and squeeze it out through spinnerets. In an orb web, the spokes are dry, but the spiral threads are coated in glue.

why.q: Why do octopuses squirt ink?
why.a: Ink is an escape trick. An octopus keeps a sac of dark ink, colored by melanin, the same stuff that darkens your skin in the sun. If a predator lunges, the octopus fires the ink out and jets away.

why.q: Why does a whale blow a spout of mist when it surfaces?
why.a: That misty spout is mostly breath, not water. A whale holds its breath underwater, then surfaces and blows out hard through the blowhole on top of its head. The air from its lungs is warm and damp, so when it hits cooler outside air it turns into a cloud of tiny droplets, just like your breath on a frosty morning.

why.q: Why do some deep-sea animals glow in the dark?
why.a: Sunlight never reaches the deep ocean, so animals make their own light. Inside their bodies a chemical called luciferin mixes with oxygen and gives off a cold glow, usually blue. This is bioluminescence, and most deep-sea animals can do it.

why.q: Why do Venus flytraps snap shut when a fly lands on them?
why.a: Venus flytraps grow in soggy, sour bog soil that is short on nitrogen, the nutrient plants need to build proteins. So they catch their nitrogen instead. Each trap has tiny trigger hairs, and it needs two electrical signals before it fires.

why.q: Why do sunflowers follow the Sun?
why.a: Young sunflowers really do. A growing sunflower's stem grows faster on its east side during the day, tipping the bud west to follow the Sun, then grows faster on the west side at night to swing it back east before dawn. An inner body clock keeps the rhythm.

why.q: Why do we yawn?
why.a: Nobody knows for sure. Scientists once thought yawning pulled in extra oxygen, but experiments disproved that: giving people extra oxygen did not stop them yawning, and short-changing them on oxygen did not make them yawn more. One idea is that a yawn helps cool your brain, because the big jaw stretch and a deep breath of cool air change the blood flow in your head.

why.q: Why do our fingers wrinkle in the bath?
why.a: Not because your skin soaks up water like a sponge. It is your nervous system doing it on purpose. Water seeps into the sweat pores, upsets the salt balance, and nerves signal tiny blood vessels in your fingertips to narrow.

why.q: Why does pepper make us sneeze?
why.a: Ground pepper contains a chemical called piperine. Breathe in a puff and the tiny grains land on the wet lining inside your nose, where piperine tickles sensitive nerve endings that normally warn you about heat and harsh chemicals. Those nerves fire an alarm to a sneeze center in your brainstem.

why.q: Why do we hiccup?
why.a: A hiccup starts with a sudden twitch of your diaphragm, the big breathing muscle under your lungs, and the muscles between your ribs twitch with it. That twitch yanks air in fast. A moment later your vocal cords, two stretchy bands inside your voice box, snap shut and stop the air.

why.q: Why does your tummy rumble?
why.a: Your stomach and intestines are long, hollow, muscular tubes. To move a meal along they squeeze in slow waves called peristalsis. Doctors call the sound borborygmi.

why.q: Why do we cry when we are sad?
why.a: Sadness switches on nerves that run to the tear glands above your eyes, so they make extra tears. Emotional tears are set off by your feelings, not by dust or onion fumes, though the same glands make both. Scientists have the clearest evidence that crying works as a signal: people who see your tears treat you more kindly and are more willing to help.

why.q: Why does being tickled make us laugh?
why.a: Being tickled sets off a burst of laughter that is not quite the same as laughing at a joke. Scientists still argue about why. Some think it is a reflex that guards ticklish spots like the ribs, neck, and armpits.

why.q: Why do we feel dizzy after spinning around?
why.a: Deep inside each ear are three tiny loops called semicircular canals, filled with liquid. When you spin, the liquid swirls and bends tiny hairs inside, and those hairs tell your brain you are turning. Here is the trick: when you stop, the liquid keeps sloshing, and it can take fifteen or twenty seconds to settle down.

why.q: Why do we shiver when we are cold?
why.a: Your body works best at about 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit, so a control center in your brain called the hypothalamus watches your temperature closely. When you get too cold, it orders your muscles to twitch, tightening and loosening many times a second. You cannot stop it, because you are not the one giving the order.

why.q: Why do cuts grow a scab?
why.a: Cut yourself and blood leaks out, so your body plugs the hole fast. Tiny sticky pieces of blood called platelets rush over and clump together, while a stringy protein called fibrin weaves a net that traps them. That is a clot.

why.q: Why does a bruise turn purple and then yellow?
why.a: A bump can break the tiny blood vessels just under your skin without breaking the skin itself. Blood leaks out and gets trapped, and that pooled blood looks red, then purple through the skin. Your body then cleans up the mess.

why.q: Why does a haircut not hurt?
why.a: Hair grows from a tiny pocket in your skin called a follicle. Down at the bottom, living cells divide and pile up. As they get pushed upward they fill with a tough protein called keratin and die.

why.q: Why do our fingernails keep growing?
why.a: Under the base of each nail is a patch of living skin called the matrix. It makes new cells all the time. As fresh cells pile up they flatten, harden with keratin, and die, pushing the older ones forward over your fingertip.

why.q: Why does food taste boring when you have a cold?
why.a: Most of what you call taste is really smell. Your tongue only detects a few basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and savory. While you chew, smells drift up a channel from the back of your throat into your nose, where smell receptors read them.

why.q: Why do we burp?
why.a: Every time you swallow food or a drink, you swallow air too. That air collects in your stomach and stretches it. When the stomach has had enough, a ring of muscle at the bottom of your food pipe relaxes and lets the gas rush back up and out of your mouth as a burp.

why.q: Why do we feel hungry?
why.a: Hunger is a message from your body, not just your stomach. When your stomach is empty, it makes a hormone called ghrelin and sends it into your blood. Ghrelin travels to the hypothalamus, a control center deep in your brain, and tells it that fuel is running low.

why.q: Why does your heart beat faster when you run?
why.a: Working muscles burn fuel, and burning fuel needs oxygen. Your blood carries oxygen, so when you run, your muscles need much more blood than usual. Your heart answers by beating faster and squeezing harder, pumping several times more blood every minute.

why.q: Why do we have two eyes instead of one?
why.a: Your eyes sit a couple of inches apart, so each one sees the world from a slightly different angle. Your brain compares the two pictures and fuses them into one. The small differences between them, called disparity, tell it how far away things are, which is why you can catch a ball or pour a drink.

why.q: Why do our ears pop on a plane?
why.a: Your eardrum has air on both sides: air in the outside world and air in the middle ear behind it. A thin passage called the eustachian tube runs from your middle ear to the back of your nose and keeps those two pressures matched. When a plane climbs or drops, the outside pressure changes fast and the tube cannot keep up, so your ear feels blocked.

why.q: Why do we grow taller?
why.a: Near the ends of your long bones, like your thigh bone, sit growth plates made of soft cartilage. Cells there keep dividing and pushing the ends apart, and the old cartilage behind them hardens into solid bone. That is how your legs and arms get longer, so you get taller.

why.q: Why does popcorn pop?
why.a: Inside every popcorn kernel is a tiny drop of water surrounded by soft starch, all sealed in a very tough hull. When the kernel gets hot, that water turns to steam. The strong hull traps the steam, so pressure builds and builds.

why.q: Why do computers use only ones and zeros?
why.a: Inside a computer are billions of tiny switches called transistors. A switch is easy to build and easy to read, because it is either on or off, with nothing in between. Even if the electricity wobbles a little, a computer can still tell on from off, so it almost never makes mistakes.

why.q: Why does lightning happen?
why.a: Inside a tall storm cloud, ice crystals and soft hailstones crash into each other in strong winds. These collisions move electric charge around: the heavier bits fall and take negative charge low in the cloud, while light ice crystals carry positive charge high up. Air normally blocks electricity, but when the charges get big enough, the air gives way and a giant spark leaps out.

why.q: Why does a heavy ship float when a coin sinks?
why.a: Anything in water is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the water it shoves aside. A coin is small and solid, so it pushes aside only a spoonful of water. That tiny push is weaker than the coin's weight, and down it goes.

why.q: Why does a magnet stick to the fridge?
why.a: Most refrigerator doors are made of steel, and steel is mostly iron. Inside iron are countless tiny magnetic regions called domains, pointing every which way, so they cancel out. Bring a magnet close and those domains swing around to line up with it.

why.q: Why does bread rise?
why.a: Yeast is a living thing, a fungus so small you need a microscope to see it. Mixed into dough, yeast eats sugars from the flour and breathes out carbon dioxide gas. Kneading builds a stretchy web of protein called gluten, and that web traps the gas as thousands of tiny bubbles.

why.q: Why do bubbles always come out round?
why.a: The skin of a bubble is a thin sheet of soapy water, and water pulls on itself. That pull, called surface tension, squeezes the film to make it as small as it can be. A ball is the shape that wraps a puff of air in the least skin, so a floating bubble settles into a sphere.

why.q: Why does glass break so easily?
why.a: Glass is a solid whose atoms are jumbled in a random pattern, locked in place with no neat rows. It is not flowing; it is solid. In metals, layers of atoms can slide and bend to absorb a blow.

why.q: Why do clocks run clockwise?
why.a: Long before machines told time, people used sundials. A stick's shadow swings around as the Sun crosses the sky. North of the equator that shadow sweeps from left to right, past the same points in the same order every day.

why.q: Why does a microwave heat your food?
why.a: A microwave oven makes invisible radio-type waves with a part called a magnetron. Water molecules are lopsided: one end is a little positive, the other a little negative. The wave's electric field flips direction billions of times a second, and the water molecules twist back and forth to follow it.

why.q: Why does a bicycle stay upright when you ride it?
why.a: Balancing a bike is like balancing a broom on your hand: when it starts to fall, you move the base back underneath it. A rider does that by steering into the lean, mostly without thinking. A moving bike can do it alone, because leaning makes the front wheel turn.

why.q: Why do we hear thunder after we see lightning?
why.a: Lightning heats the air in its channel to about 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit in an instant. That air explodes outward, then snaps back, and the shock wave spreads out as the boom we call thunder. The flash and the boom start together.

why.q: Why does a phone screen know you are touching it?
why.a: A phone screen is not feeling a push. Under the glass sits a grid of see-through wires holding a weak electric field. Your body conducts electricity, so when a finger comes close, it changes how much charge that spot can hold.

why.q: Why do wheels make things easier to pull?
why.a: Dragging a heavy box means its whole bottom scrapes along the ground, and that scraping, called sliding friction, fights you the entire way. A wheel is cleverer: it rolls. The patch touching the ground is standing still for an instant, so nothing scrapes there and far less energy is wasted.

why.q: Why does a balloon stick to your hair?
why.a: Rubbing a balloon on your head drags tiny particles called electrons off your hair and onto the balloon. The balloon collects extra electrons and becomes negatively charged, while your hair, now missing some, becomes positively charged. Opposite charges pull toward each other, so your hair lifts up and clings.

why.q: Why does hot air rise?
why.a: Heat makes air spread out, so a warm patch of air has fewer molecules in the same space. That makes it less dense, meaning lighter for its size. The cooler air around it is denser, and gravity pulls it down harder.

why.q: Why does a light bulb glow?
why.a: An old-style bulb holds a hair-thin metal wire called a filament. Electricity pushing through it heats that wire to thousands of degrees, and metal that hot shines white, like a glowing ember. Scientists call this incandescence.

why.q: Why does a spinning top stay upright?
why.a: A spinning top has angular momentum, the stubbornness of anything turning fast. Its spin axis wants to keep pointing the same direction unless a twisting force changes it. Gravity does try to tip the top over, but instead of falling it answers sideways: the axis swings slowly around in a circle, which scientists call precession.

why.q: Why does metal feel colder than wood?
why.a: It isn't colder. A metal spoon and a wooden spoon sitting in the same room are exactly the same temperature. The trick is that your skin cannot measure an object's temperature, only its own.

why.q: Why does a mirror swap your left and right?
why.a: It doesn't. A mirror flips front and back, along the line pointing straight at the glass. Your nose in the reflection points back toward you, while up stays up and your left side stays on your left side.

why.q: Why is the sea salty?
why.a: Rain falling on land is slightly acidic, because it picks up carbon dioxide from the air. That weak acid slowly wears away rock and frees tiny particles called ions. Rivers carry those ions down to the sea.

why.q: Why do we have tides?
why.a: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans. Water on the side facing the Moon is pulled hardest and bulges out. On the opposite side the Moon's pull is weakest, so water is left behind there and bulges out too.

why.q: Why is the deep sea so dark?
why.a: Sunlight is soaked up by water. Red light disappears first, then the other colors, so the light fades fast as you go down. The top 650 feet is the sunlight zone.

why.q: Why can whales hold their breath so long?
why.a: A whale's big lungs are not the main trick. Its blood and muscles are loaded with special proteins that grab and hold oxygen, so a diving whale carries a large store inside its body. The muscle protein is called myoglobin.

why.q: Why do jellyfish sting?
why.a: A jellyfish tentacle is covered with tiny stinging cells, each holding a coiled, venom-tipped thread under huge pressure. Touch it and the thread shoots out in a fraction of a second. The cell fires by itself; it is a hunting tool for catching small drifting animals.

why.q: Why do crabs walk sideways?
why.a: A crab's legs come out from the sides of its wide, flat shell. Each leg joint bends one way only, like a door hinge, and in most crabs those hinges give their biggest, strongest swing out to the side. So left and right is the easy, powerful direction, and forwards is the awkward one.

why.q: Why do dolphins leap out of the water?
why.a: Nobody is certain, and scientists think there are several reasons. Leaping may shake off itchy parasites clinging to the skin. It may be a signal to other dolphins, since a big splash carries a long way underwater.

why.q: Why do seashells wash up empty?
why.a: A seashell is not a home someone moved out of. It is the skeleton of a soft animal called a mollusk, such as a snail, clam, or oyster. A body layer called the mantle builds the shell from calcium carbonate, the mineral in chalk.

why.q: Why does the sea look blue?
why.a: Water is not just a clear window for light. When sunlight shines into the sea, water soaks up the long wavelengths first, so red, orange, then yellow and green disappear within a few yards. Blue light has short wavelengths, so it travels deepest and gets scattered back to your eyes.

why.q: Why do seahorses look so strange?
why.a: Seahorses are true fish, but they break most of the fish rules. Instead of scales they wear rings of bony armor, so they swim upright and slowly, fluttering one small fin on the back. A curling tail grips seagrass like a monkey's tail, and a tube-shaped snout sucks up tiny shrimp.

why.q: Why can an octopus squeeze through a tiny gap?
why.a: An octopus has no bones at all. Its arms and body are pure muscle, so they can stretch, fold, and flatten into almost any shape. The one hard piece is its beak, a parrot-like tool in the middle of the arms that it uses to crack shells.

why.q: Why is the water at the bottom of the sea so cold?
why.a: Sunlight only warms the top of the ocean, and hardly any of it reaches below about 650 feet, so everything deeper stays dark, far from any sunshine. The cold water down there did not start at the bottom, either. Near the poles, surface water loses its heat to the freezing air.

why.q: Why do sea turtles come back to the same beach?
why.a: Female sea turtles usually nest on the same stretch of coast where they hatched, sometimes after crossing an entire ocean. Scientists think they use Earth's magnetic field like a map. Every beach has a slightly different magnetic signature, and a hatchling seems to memorize its home signature, then steer back to it decades later.

why.q: Why do puffins carry so many fish at once?
why.a: A puffin is flying food home to one chick in a burrow, and a single fish would hardly be worth the trip. So it catches several on one dive and holds them crosswise. Backward-facing spines on the roof of its mouth grip each slippery fish while its rough, rasping tongue presses them in place, so the puffin can open its bill and grab another without dropping the rest.

why.q: Why is the ocean floor not flat?
why.a: Earth's crust is cracked into giant moving plates, and that movement builds the sea floor. Where plates pull apart, hot rock piles up into the mid-ocean ridge, a volcanic mountain chain about 40,000 miles long. Where one plate dives under another, the floor bends down into a trench.

why.q: Why does a whale sing?
why.a: Male humpback whales are the singers. One song usually lasts under ten minutes, and the whale repeats it again and again, sometimes for hours without stopping. Scientists think singing is mainly a way for a grown male to advertise himself to females.

why.q: Why do barnacles stick to ships?
why.a: A barnacle begins as a tiny swimming larva hunting for something hard to live on forever. When it finds a good surface it settles head-down and glues itself with a natural cement, among the strongest glues known, then builds a shell of chalky plates around itself. A ship's hull is simply a very good hard surface that moves through food-filled water.

why.q: Why do penguins not freeze?
why.a: A penguin wears short, stiff feathers that overlap like roof tiles, with fluffy down underneath. The outer layer sheds water, and the down holds a blanket of trapped air that heat struggles to cross. Below the skin lies thick fat.

why.q: Why does an eel give a shock?
why.a: An electric eel is not a true eel at all. It is a South American knifefish, and about four fifths of its long body is electric organs. Those organs are thousands of flat, modified muscle cells stacked in rows like batteries in a flashlight.

why.q: Why have we explored so little of the ocean?
why.a: Because it is huge, pitch dark and crushingly deep, and every visit needs a ship, a robot or a submarine. Sonar mapping from ships had covered about 28.7 percent of the world's sea floor in modern detail by 2026; that gives us its shape, not a look at it. Actually seeing the deep sea floor is far rarer.

why.q: Why did dinosaurs get so big?
why.a: No single reason explains it, but scientists point to a package of features. Dinosaurs stood with straight, pillar-like legs under the body, so their skeletons carried huge weight. The biggest, the sauropods, had hollow, air-filled bones and bird-like air sacs that kept oxygen flowing even while breathing out.

why.q: Why do we find dinosaur bones in rock?
why.a: When a dinosaur died, its soft parts usually rotted away. Only if mud or sand buried the body quickly did the bones stand a chance. Layer after layer of sediment piled on top and hardened into sedimentary rock.

why.q: Why did some dinosaurs have feathers?
why.a: Feathers came long before flight. Many dinosaurs that could never fly wore them, starting as simple hair-like fuzz. Living birds use feathers for warmth, for showing off to mates and rivals, and for camouflage, and scientists think those were the earliest jobs too.

why.q: Why did Stegosaurus have plates on its back?
why.a: Its plates were not attached to the skeleton; they were set into the skin along its back. Scientists are not certain what they were for. Display is the leading idea: showing off to mates or warning rivals, or letting stegosaurs recognize each other.

why.q: Why did Triceratops have horns?
why.a: Triceratops had two long brow horns, a short nose horn, and a big bony frill. Movie fights against T. rex are not the main answer.

why.q: Why did some dinosaurs eat stones?
why.a: Stones swallowed on purpose are called gastroliths, and they really do turn up inside fossil skeletons. In birds today, swallowed grit sits in a muscular gizzard and grinds tough food. People assumed sauropods did the same, but a study weighing ostrich stones showed sauropods carried far too few for that job.

why.q: Why do we keep finding new dinosaurs?
why.a: Because the rocks keep giving them up. Wind, rain and ice wear hillsides down and expose fresh bone, so a fossil hidden for a hundred million years can appear this year. Hunters are also digging in places that were barely searched before, and Africa and India look like the richest ground still to come.

why.q: Why did pterosaurs fly if they were not birds?
why.a: Pterosaurs were flying reptiles. They were not birds and not dinosaurs, and they have no close living relatives. Their wing was not made of feathers.

why.q: Why do some fossils show footprints?
why.a: A footprint is a trace fossil. It records something an animal did, not a piece of its body. An animal stepped in soft mud or sand, the prints dried and hardened, and more sediment buried them until everything turned to rock.

why.q: Why did woolly mammoths have such long hair?
why.a: Long hair on its own would not keep anything warm. A woolly mammoth wore a whole cold-weather outfit. Long outer hairs, some of them close to three feet, lay over a dense woolly undercoat that trapped warm air against the skin, and under that sat a thick layer of fat.

why.q: Why did sabre toothed cats have those teeth?
why.a: Those long canines were slicing knives, not crowbars. They were flattened, very sharp, and surprisingly easy to snap, so hitting bone or a twisting animal could break them. Scientists think a saber-toothed cat used its powerful front legs to pin large prey still, then drove the teeth into the soft throat in one deep slicing bite.

why.q: Why did the first fish crawl onto land?
why.a: They were not ordinary fish. Lobe-finned fish had thick muscly fins with real bones inside, arranged one bone, then two bones, then a bunch of small ones. Those are the same bones as your upper arm, forearm, and wrist.

why.q: Why were there giant dragonflies?
why.a: Giant griffinflies, cousins of today's dragonflies, had wings spanning up to twenty-eight inches, roughly your outstretched arms. They hunted on the wing about three hundred million years ago, when Earth's air held much more oxygen than it does now. Insects do not have lungs.

why.q: Why do scientists argue about dinosaur colors?
why.a: Some fossils keep tiny structures called melanosomes, the little packets that hold dark pigment. Scientists compare their shapes with those in living birds and work out a color. That gave Psittacosaurus a dark back and a pale belly, good camouflage.

why.q: Why did some dinosaurs have crests on their heads?
why.a: Different dinosaurs, different reasons. Many crests were showing-off gear. The newly named Spinosaurus mirabilis carried a sword-shaped crest that helped it attract mates and warn off rivals, like a cassowary's helmet today.

why.q: Why did Diplodocus have such a long neck and tail?
why.a: A long neck was a feeding machine. Standing still, Diplodocus could sweep its small head over a huge patch of ferns and low branches without moving its heavy body, which saved energy. Air spaces in the bones kept the neck light.

why.q: Why do we name dinosaurs in Latin?
why.a: Every animal, living or extinct, gets a two-part scientific name built from Latin and Greek roots, like Tyrannosaurus rex. Those languages belong to no country today, so the name means the same to a scientist in Tokyo, Lagos, or Chicago. One animal, one name, no confusion.

why.q: Why did humans survive when so many animals did not?
why.a: Humans were the odd ones out. The wave of extinctions hit giants hardest, and only 11 of 57 kinds of plant-eater over a ton survive today. Scientists find pressure from people, above all hunting, was the main driver.

why.q: Why is coal made of ancient forests?
why.a: Dead plants usually rot, because bacteria eat them using oxygen. In a waterlogged peat bog the standing water runs out of oxygen, so decay almost stops and plant material piles up as peat. Bury that peat under layers of mud and rock and the weight squeezes the water out, while deep heat cooks what is left.

why.q: Why will we never bring dinosaurs back?
why.a: DNA falls apart. Measured in 158 moa bones, a short piece of DNA had a half-life of about 521 years: half the copies break every 521 years, then half of what is left, again and again. After a few million years nothing readable remains.

why.q: Why does it rain?
why.a: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets, far too small and light to fall. Each one formed when water vapor cooled and condensed onto a speck of dust, salt or pollen. Inside the cloud the droplets keep bumping into each other and joining up, and ice crystals can grow fast and then melt on the way down.

why.q: Why does snow fall instead of rain?
why.a: High inside a cloud it is usually below freezing, so most precipitation starts out as ice crystals. If the air below stays cold enough, the crystals reach the ground still frozen, as snow. They can even survive a degree or two above freezing, because melting chills the air right around them.

why.q: Why is every snowflake different?
why.a: A snowflake starts as a single ice crystal and grows as water vapor freezes onto it. Its branches answer the exact temperature and dampness it passes through, and no two flakes take the same path down. Because one flake holds an enormous number of water molecules, the possible arrangements are almost beyond counting.

why.q: Why does the wind blow?
why.a: Air presses down on everything, and it presses harder in some places than others. The sun heats the ground unevenly. Where air is warmed it rises, leaving fewer air molecules and lower pressure behind, while elsewhere air sinks and packs together into higher pressure.

why.q: Why do hurricanes spin?
why.a: A hurricane is built around a center of very low pressure, so air rushes in toward it from every direction. Earth is turning underneath that moving air, which bends its path to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern. This is called the Coriolis effect, and it curls the incoming air into a huge spiral rather than a straight rush.

why.q: Why is it colder at the top of a mountain?
why.a: Not because you are nearer the sun. Climbing a mountain barely changes that distance at all. What changes is pressure.

why.q: Why does fog appear in the morning?
why.a: Fog is simply a cloud sitting on the ground. On a clear, calm night heat escapes easily from the land, so the air just above it cools through the small hours. Cool air can hold less water vapor, and once it reaches its dew point the vapor condenses into countless tiny droplets you can see.

why.q: Why does frost make patterns on windows?
why.a: Window frost is not frozen dew. When the glass is colder than freezing, water vapor in the air can turn straight into ice on it without ever being liquid, a change called deposition. Ice does not start just anywhere, though.

why.q: Why does it feel hotter when the air is damp?
why.a: Your main way of dumping extra heat is sweating. Sweat only cools you while it evaporates, because changing liquid into vapor carries energy off your skin. When the air already holds plenty of water vapor, evaporation slows to a crawl, so the heat stays inside you.

why.q: Why does the sky go yellow before a storm?
why.a: A storm cloud can be miles deep, so almost all the sunlight entering the top is scattered or soaked up before it reaches the base, which looks nearly black. Big storms often build late in the day, when sunlight takes a long slanting path through the air and turns yellow. That warm light under a black cloud is the yellow you see.

why.q: Why do we get thunderstorms in summer?
why.a: Thunderstorms need warm, damp air that can rise quickly. In summer the sun heats the ground hard, the ground heats the air just above it, and that warm air is lighter than its surroundings, so it climbs. Rising air cools, its vapor condenses, and a towering cumulonimbus cloud grows.

why.q: Why does it never rain in some places?
why.a: The very driest places have several dry-makers stacked on top of each other. Chile's Atacama sits under the sinking air of a stubborn high-pressure area, behind the Andes, and beside the cold Humboldt current, which chills the sea so little water evaporates from it. Three blocks at once leave almost nothing left to rain out.

why.q: Why do monsoons happen every year?
why.a: A monsoon is a whole wind system that flips with the seasons, giving a soaking wet half-year and a dry one. People once explained it as a giant sea breeze, with land heating faster than ocean in summer and pulling in wet sea air. That does matter, but scientists now describe monsoons mainly through the tropical rain belt, where air rises near the equator and shifts north or south each year as the strongest sunshine moves.

why.q: Why do the seasons come at different times around the world?
why.a: Earth spins on an axis that leans over by about 23.5 degrees, and that lean keeps pointing the same way all year. In June the northern half tips toward the Sun and catches its rays more directly, so the north has summer while the south has winter. Six months later the two swap over.

why.q: Why is the Arctic ice melting?
why.a: The Arctic is warming faster than the rest of the planet, so more sea ice melts each summer than the winter can replace. Bright ice reflects sunlight back to space, but dark open water soaks the heat up, which melts still more ice. In September 2025 the floating ice shrank to 4.60 million square kilometers, sharing tenth lowest place in the 47 year satellite record.

why.q: Why does lightning strike tall things?
why.a: Inside a storm cloud, colliding ice and hail leave the cloud base strongly negative. That negative charge pushes electrons down and away in the ground below, leaving the surface and everything standing on it positively charged. The spark then forms along the shortest, easiest path between cloud and ground.

why.q: Why does a rainbow make an arc?
why.a: Sunlight entering a raindrop bends, bounces off the back of the drop, and bends again coming out, splitting into colors as it goes. The light leaves at roughly 40 to 42 degrees from the direction it came in. So a drop only lights up for you if it sits at that angle from the point straight opposite the Sun, which is the shadow of your own head.

why.q: Why do earthquakes happen?
why.a: The outside of the Earth is broken into huge slabs called plates that creep slowly past and into each other. Where two slabs meet, the rough edges snag and lock while the rest of the rock keeps being pushed along, so strain builds up around the crack, which is called a fault. Eventually the stuck part gives way and jerks free.

why.q: Why does a tsunami travel so fast?
why.a: An ordinary wave only stirs the top of the sea. A tsunami is a shove given to the whole depth of the ocean at once, usually by an earthquake on the sea floor, and a wave like that travels at a speed set by how deep the water is. The deeper the water, the faster it goes.

why.q: Why do rivers bend instead of running straight?
why.a: No riverbed is perfectly even, so the flow always leans to one side somewhere. On the outside of that curve the water runs faster and scrapes the bank away. On the inside it runs slower and drops the sand and grit it was carrying.

why.q: Why does bread go stale?
why.a: Stale bread is not simply dry bread. Baking makes the starch inside soak up water and unwind. As the loaf sits, those starch molecules slowly line up again into tiny crystals and push water away, so the crumb turns firm and crumbly.

why.q: Why do onions make you cry?
why.a: An onion stores a sulfur chemical in one part of its cells and the enzymes that attack it in another. Your knife breaks those walls, the two mix, and within seconds the onion builds a gas called propanethial S-oxide. It drifts upward and lands on the wet surface of your eyes, where it irritates the nerve endings there.

why.q: Why does chocolate melt in your mouth?
why.a: Chocolate is made of cocoa butter, sugar and ground cocoa, and it is the cocoa butter, the fat, that does the melting. That fat is unusual: it can set into six different crystal forms, each with its own melting point. Makers work hard to build only the best one, form five, through careful heating and cooling called tempering.

why.q: Why does milk go sour?
why.a: Milk always carries some bacteria, and a few kinds keep growing slowly even in a cold fridge. They feed on lactose, the sugar in milk, and give off lactic acid. That acid is the sour taste and smell, and it also makes the milk's protein clump into lumps instead of staying smooth.

why.q: Why does cheese smell so strong?
why.a: Cheese begins as milk, then bacteria, molds and enzymes spend weeks or months taking that milk apart. They chop its proteins and fats into hundreds of smaller pieces, and many of those pieces are light enough to drift into the air and reach your nose. The ones built around sulfur smell especially powerful.

why.q: Why does meat change color when it cooks?
why.a: Muscle holds a red protein called myoglobin, which stores oxygen for the living animal. That protein, not blood, is what makes raw meat red and what colors the juice in the pan. Heat pulls its carefully folded shape apart, which changes how it handles light, so red fades to pink and then to grey-brown.

why.q: Why does a cake rise in the oven?
why.a: Three things lift a cake together. Baking powder reacts in the wet batter and releases carbon dioxide, which feeds into the air bubbles that beating already whipped in. Oven heat makes that gas expand and turns water in the batter into steam, stretching the bubbles wider.

why.q: Why does ice cream go icy in the freezer?
why.a: Ice cream does not dry out. Fresh from the machine it holds millions of ice crystals so tiny your tongue reads them as smooth. Every time the tub warms a little, on the way home or when the freezer door opens, some ice melts.

why.q: Why does salt make food taste better?
why.a: Salt is sodium chloride. Cells on your tongue react to sodium and give you the salty taste, but salt does far more than that. A little salt hides bitterness and makes sweet things taste sweeter, and it helps smell molecules escape the food and reach your nose, so the whole mouthful seems fuller.

why.q: Why does mint feel cold?
why.a: Mint contains menthol. Your nerves carry a receptor called TRPM8 that normally opens when things get cool, below roughly 77 degrees Fahrenheit, and reports cold to your brain. Menthol opens that same receptor without changing the temperature at all, so the message says cold when nothing has cooled.

why.q: Why does lemon make your mouth water?
why.a: Lemon juice is packed with citric acid, and acids taste sour. Taste cells on your tongue spot the acid and send signals down to a small group of cells in your brain stem that controls your salivary glands. Those glands switch on hard, and your mouth floods with saliva that waters the acid down and soaks up the sourness.

why.q: Why does food taste different when it is cold?
why.a: Temperature changes two things at once. First the smell. Aroma molecules creep out of cold food slowly and pour out as it warms, and most of what you call flavor is really smell.

why.q: Why does honey never go off?
why.a: Honey holds very little water, and the enormous amount of sugar grabs hold of what water there is. A bacterium landing in honey has water dragged straight out of its body, so it cannot grow. Honey is acidic too, and bees add an enzyme that slowly makes tiny amounts of hydrogen peroxide, a mild germ-killer.

why.q: Why does frying make food crispy?
why.a: Hot oil carries heat straight into the food's surface, so that surface heats fast. The water there boils away as steam, and a thin outer layer dries out and turns hard and brittle. That dried layer is the crunch you hear.

why.q: Why does a potato go green?
why.a: Potatoes grow underground in the dark. When light reaches one, the skin starts making chlorophyll, the same green coloring that leaves use. The green itself is not poisonous, but the same light switches on a separate bitter chemical called solanine, which can make you ill.

why.q: Why does pasta water boil over?
why.a: Plain water boils in bubbles that pop the moment they reach the surface. Pasta changes that. As it cooks, starch leaks out of the pasta and dissolves in the water.

why.q: Why does a fridge stop food going bad?
why.a: A fridge does not kill anything. It only makes life slow. Bacteria and molds grow on food, and the food's own chemical reactions keep changing it, but both slow down a lot in the cold.

why.q: Why does bubblegum never dissolve?
why.a: Gum is two things mixed together. The sweet part, the sugar and flavoring, dissolves in your spit, so gum goes tasteless after a few minutes. What is left is the gum base, a rubbery mix of gums, waxes and plastics that your body cannot break down.

why.q: Why is popcorn the only corn that pops?
why.a: Every dried corn kernel holds a little water. Heat turns that water to steam, and steam needs far more room than water does. Popcorn is built to trap it: a thick, tough hull outside and hard, glassy starch inside.

why.q: Why do we get a full feeling after eating?
why.a: Your stomach wall has stretch sensors. As it fills, they send a message to your brain along a nerve. At the same time your gut squirts out hormones with names like CCK, GLP-1 and PYY, which also tell the brain that food has arrived.

why.q: Why do we forget things?
why.a: Forgetting is normal, and your brain does some of it on purpose. It is not a broken machine. Scientists have found the brain uses active processes that weaken memories it does not seem to need, sorting them by how useful or important they are.

why.q: Why do we get scared of the dark?
why.a: In the dark your eyes stop giving your brain the information it normally uses. You cannot check whether the shape by the door is a coat or something else, so your brain plays it safe and stays on alert. People jump harder at a sudden noise in the dark than in the light.

why.q: Why is yawning catching?
why.a: Yawning spreads. Seeing someone yawn, hearing one, or even reading about yawning can set you off. What scientists cannot agree on is why.

why.q: Why do our eyes play tricks on us?
why.a: Your eyes do not send a finished picture to your brain. They send patches of light, dark and color, and your brain builds its best guess about what is out there, using shortcuts and what usually turns out to be true. Most of the time the guess is right.

why.q: Why does time feel slow when you are bored?
why.a: Time is not something you can see or hear, so your brain works it out. When you are busy, attention goes to the task. When you are bored, there is little else to spend it on, so you spend it on time itself.

why.q: Why does a song get stuck in your head?
why.a: A song stuck on repeat in your head has a name in research: involuntary musical imagery, or an earworm. Studies find that most people get them, that they are usually a short piece of a tune rather than the whole song, and that they often follow hearing that music recently or many times. Something can also trigger one, like a word from the lyrics.

why.q: Why do we laugh?
why.a: Laughing is mostly something we do with other people, and not only at jokes. Researchers who studied hundreds of recorded laughs found that listeners hear different messages in them: this is fun, we are friends, or I am the one in charge. Laughter is also older than words.

why.q: Why do we get angry?
why.a: Anger usually turns up when something blocks you or when somebody treats you unfairly. It feels bad, but it does not make you back away. Researchers group anger with the feelings that push you towards a problem instead of away from it, which is why anger makes you want to do something.

why.q: Why can we not tickle ourselves?
why.a: Scientists think that when you move, your brain works out in advance what that movement will feel like, and the cerebellum at the base of the brain helps do it. Touch that matches the prediction gets turned down, so your own fingers feel dull instead of ticklish. The rule is not perfect.

why.q: Why do we copy other people without noticing?
why.a: People copy each other without meaning to. In a well-known experiment, the person sitting with you rubbed their face or jiggled their foot, and you began doing the same, then said afterwards that you had not noticed. Researchers call this the chameleon effect.

why.q: Why do we have a favorite color?
why.a: People do have steady favourite colours, but where a favourite comes from is not settled. One idea is that you like a colour because you like the things it reminds you of. That idea fits American choices well and Saudi choices much less well, so it is not the whole story.

why.q: Why can we recognize a face so fast?
why.a: Faces get their own machinery. Patches of the brain, including one called the fusiform face area, react far more strongly to faces than to other things you look at. And it is quick.

why.q: Why do we see faces in clouds?
why.a: Your face detector is quick rather than careful. Any pattern with two dots above a line can set it off, so a cloud, a socket or a car turns into a face. Researchers call this pareidolia.

why.q: Why do we cry at films?
why.a: The story is invented, but your feelings about it are not. When a character is built well, you take their point of view and feel their emotions almost as if they were your own. Your body joins in.

why.q: Why does hearing your own voice sound wrong?
why.a: When you talk, the sound reaches your inner ear by two routes at once: through the air, and straight through the bones of your skull. The bone route pushes the low, deep tones forward, so your voice sounds lower and fuller to you than it does to anybody else. A microphone only catches the air part.

why.q: Why do we dream about falling?
why.a: Two different things get mixed up here. A hypnic jerk is a sudden twitch of the whole body just as you drop off, in the first stage of sleep, sometimes with a strong sense of falling. Around seven in ten people have had one.

why.q: Why does counting sheep not really work?
why.a: The idea is that counting crowds worries out of your head. The evidence is thin and rests on one small study of 41 people with trouble sleeping. Those told to picture an interesting, absorbing scene fell asleep sooner.

why.q: Why do crowds change how people behave?
why.a: In a crowd you stop acting only as yourself and start acting as part of a group, and that shifts what feels like the normal thing to do. The old story says a crowd becomes a mindless mob that panics. Researchers who study real emergencies find the opposite is far more usual: strangers cooperate and help one another.

why.q: Why do we find baby animals cute?
why.a: Because they match a pattern our brains are tuned to. Scientists call it the baby schema: a large forehead, big eyes, and a small nose and mouth. In one brain scan study, young women looking at faces with more of this pattern showed activity in the nucleus accumbens, part of the brain's reward system, the machinery that makes things feel good.

why.q: Why is it so hard to change a habit?
why.a: Because a habit is not a decision. Repeat an action after the same cue, such as brushing your teeth after breakfast, and it starts running by itself, before you have thought about it. Replacing it means building a whole new automatic response.

why.q: Why does a crane not tip over?
why.a: A crane stays up because the turning force from its load is always kept smaller than the turning force holding it down. A load pushes down at a distance from the base, and weight times distance gives a tipping moment. Engineers balance that with a heavy counterweight behind the mast and a wide base, spread even wider by outriggers on truck cranes.

why.q: Why do trains run on rails?
why.a: Steel wheels on steel rails barely squash each other, so very little energy is lost as they roll. That low rolling resistance is why one engine can pull a heavy freight train. The rails also steer it.

why.q: Why does a submarine sink and rise again?
why.a: A submarine floats when the water it pushes aside weighs more than the submarine does. To dive, the crew opens valves and lets seawater flood into ballast tanks, which adds weight without adding size, so the boat becomes heavy enough to sink. To come back up, compressed air is blown into those tanks and pushes the water out, so the submarine is light again and rises.

why.q: Why do rockets fall away in stages?
why.a: Most of a rocket at liftoff is fuel, held in big heavy tanks. Once a tank is empty, the metal around it is dead weight, and lifting dead weight wastes fuel. So the rocket drops the empty stage and lights a smaller engine on what is left.

why.q: Why does a digger have tracks instead of wheels?
why.a: A digger is heavy and often stands on mud, sand or broken ground. Wheels press all that weight onto a few small patches, so they sink in and spin. Tracks are long belts that spread the same weight over a much larger area of ground, so the pressure under the machine is far lower and it sinks less.

why.q: Why does a tunnel not collapse?
why.a: Digging a tunnel does not remove the weight above, it moves it. The ground around the hole presses together into an arch shape that carries the load around the opening and down the sides. Strong rock can do this on its own.

why.q: Why do skyscrapers sway in the wind?
why.a: Because they are meant to. A tall tower is slender and flexible, and wind pushes on it hard. A building stiff enough never to move would need a huge amount of extra steel, so engineers let it bend and lean a little instead, then check that people inside will not feel sick.

why.q: Why do car engines need so much oil?
why.a: Inside a running engine, metal parts slide and spin against each other thousands of times a minute. Oil keeps a slippery film between them, cutting friction and wear so the metal does not grind itself away. Oil does a second job as well: it carries heat, which is why engineers measure how well engine oil conducts heat and how much heat it can hold.

why.q: Why are electric cars so quiet?
why.a: An electric car burns no fuel, so there are no explosions in an engine and no exhaust roaring out the back. The motor simply spins, quietly and smoothly. The difference is biggest at low speed: tests found electric cars clearly quieter than gasoline cars crawling along, so United States rules now make them play a warning sound below 30 km/h, about 19 mph.

why.q: Why do planes have winglets on the tips?
why.a: Near a wingtip the air spills around the edge and rolls up into a spinning tube called a tip vortex. That swirl is what creates induced drag, and induced drag is roughly 40 percent of an airliner's total drag while it cruises. A winglet weakens the vortex, so there is less drag to push through.

why.q: Why do we still use screws and bolts?
why.a: Turning a bolt converts a small twist into a big squeeze that clamps parts together, and the clamp holds because the threads grip. The real advantage is that you can undo it. Engineers keep choosing bolted joints because they go together and come apart easily for repairs, unlike welds or glue.

why.q: Why can a computer beat a person at chess?
why.a: Chess has fixed rules and a clear goal, which suits a machine. A chess program looks ahead through enormous numbers of possible move sequences, throws away lines that neither player would choose, and scores the positions it reaches with an evaluation function. No human can calculate that fast or stay that steady for hours.

why.q: Why does artificial intelligence make mistakes?
why.a: A chatbot is not simply looking answers up in a library. Even when it searches the web, it builds its reply by predicting which words are likely to come next, using patterns from huge amounts of text. So a wrong sentence can sound just as confident as a true one, and the machine cannot reliably tell which it has produced.

why.q: Why does a phone battery get worse over time?
why.a: Inside a lithium-ion battery, a thin film keeps growing on one of the electrodes. Scientists call it the solid electrolyte interphase. Every time it thickens it locks up a little lithium for good, so less is left to carry charge.

why.q: Why do we need satellites for maps?
why.a: Every GPS satellite carries an atomic clock and broadcasts where it is and what time it is. Your phone measures how long each signal took to arrive and turns that into a distance. With signals from four satellites it works out its longitude, latitude and height.

why.q: Why do we send robots into volcanoes?
why.a: The most useful clues about a volcano are in the hot gas rising out of the crater, and that is exactly where a person cannot stand. Small uncrewed aircraft fly into the plume, sniff the carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide, and even carry bags of gas back down, while the pilot stays kilometres away. The flying is violent.

why.q: Why do 3D printers build things in layers?
why.a: A printer cannot conjure a solid shape all at once, so software slices the digital model into a stack of very thin layers. The machine then makes them one at a time, each new layer laid on top of the last and stuck to it. Because it only has to draw a flat shape at each step, the job stays simple.

why.q: Why do solar panels still work on a cloudy day?
why.a: Clouds scatter most sunlight instead of soaking it up, so light still reaches the ground from all over the sky rather than straight from the sun. Scientists call that diffuse radiation, and a solar panel can turn it into electricity. There is a catch.

why.q: Why is it hard to build a flying car?
why.a: A flying car has to be two machines at once. The air taxis being built now lift straight up like a helicopter, then fly forward on wings like an airplane, and switching between the two modes is a big part of the difficulty. The battery packs and their cooling are heavy, and that weight is a stubborn design problem.

why.q: Why do engineers test things until they break?
why.a: Because a calculation is a prediction and a broken part is a fact. Aircraft rules build that gap in deliberately: the structure must survive one and a half times the heaviest load expected in service. NASA tested two rocket skirts that way, pushing each past 140 percent of its limit load and on until it tore.

gross.q: Why do we fart?
gross.a: Farting is your body letting out gas that has built up inside you and needs a way out. Part of it is ordinary air, swallowed while you eat, drink or talk. The rest is made by bacteria living in your large intestine, whose job is to finish breaking down bits of food that your stomach and small intestine could not fully digest.

gross.q: Why do farts smell?
gross.a: Most of a fart has no smell at all. It is mostly nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, hydrogen and methane, gases that do not smell of anything on their own. The whiff comes from a tiny extra ingredient: sulphur.

gross.q: Why does eating fast make you fart and burp more?
gross.a: Every time you eat or drink, you swallow a little air, and swallowed air is one of the two main sources of gas in your gut, along with gas made by bacteria in your large intestine. Eating quickly means gulping food down before you have properly chewed it, so each rushed mouthful pulls in extra air. Some of that air comes straight back up as a burp, while the rest travels on through your gut and eventually leaves as a fart.

gross.q: Why do beans make you fart?
gross.a: Beans are full of sugars called oligosaccharides, including raffinose and stachyose, that your stomach and small intestine cannot break down on their own because they lack the right tools to digest them. So these sugars travel on, whole, into your large intestine, where huge numbers of bacteria live. The bacteria can break the sugars down through a process called fermentation, and gas is the natural result: hydrogen, carbon dioxide, methane and sometimes a little sulphur.

gross.q: Why do we burp?
gross.a: A burp is trapped air escaping the way it came in. Every time you eat or drink, you swallow a little air along with your food, and that air collects at the top of your stomach. Eating or drinking quickly, chewing gum, or sipping through a straw all make you swallow even more.

gross.q: Why do fizzy drinks make you burp more?
gross.a: Fizzy drinks are full of tiny bubbles of carbon dioxide gas, which is what makes them tingle and fizz on your tongue. When you swallow the drink, you swallow that gas too, on top of the ordinary air you always take in while drinking. All that extra gas collects in your stomach and needs somewhere to go.

gross.q: Why does everyone fart, even the Queen?
gross.a: Farting is not a bad habit or a rude accident; it is simply what happens when a digestive system does its job. Every person swallows air while eating and drinking, and every person's large intestine is home to huge numbers of bacteria that break down leftover food and make gas while they do it. That gas has to leave the body somehow, so it does, again and again, all day.

gross.q: Why do dogs fart?
gross.a: For much the same reasons people do. Every time a dog eats, it swallows a little air along with its food, and that air has to leave the body somewhere. Far more of a dog's gas comes from bacteria living in its large intestine, which break down bits of food the dog's own gut could not fully digest, releasing gas as they work.

gross.q: Why do cows burp so much, and why does that matter?
gross.a: Cows are ruminants: they have a special stomach chamber, the rumen, packed with microbes that ferment the tough grass and plants a cow eats. As those microbes break the plant matter down, they produce methane gas, and the cow has to get rid of it. Scientists who measured gas at cows' mouths and noses found that almost none comes out of the mouth: it travels up from the rumen, is diverted into the lungs, and leaves through the nostrils when the cow breathes out.

gross.q: Why can you not hold a fart in forever?
gross.a: You can hold a fart in for a while, but not forever, because part of the system is not under your control. Gas building up and stretching your rectum acts like a sudden alarm, and researchers have found that this stretch automatically relaxes your inner ring of muscle, the internal anal sphincter, through a reflex your body runs without asking you. At the same time, a separate subconscious reflex can squeeze your outer ring shut to hold things back a little longer, and you can add a conscious squeeze of your own on top of that.

gross.q: Why do farts sometimes feel warm?
gross.a: A fart is a puff of gas that has been sitting inside you. Part of it is air you swallowed; the rest was made by bacteria in your large intestine as they broke down food your stomach could not finish. Inside your body it is warm.

gross.q: Why do we fart more on aeroplanes?
gross.a: Gases squash and swell with pressure. Air pressure falls as you go higher, and an aeroplane cabin is kept at the pressure you would feel about 2,438 metres up a mountain, not at sea level. Doctors describe what happens next with a rule called Boyle's law: when the pressure around a gas drops, the gas expands.

gross.q: Why do babies fart so much?
gross.a: Newborn babies are noisy at both ends because their gut is brand new at the job. Digestion works partly by fermentation, using bacteria in the large intestine to break down leftover sugars from milk that were not fully absorbed higher up. That fermenting produces gas, and a study measuring chemicals in babies' poo found gas and bloating linked to a fermentation chemical called butyric acid, especially in the first six months, easing off by a baby's first birthday.

gross.q: Why does poo come out the shape it does?
gross.a: Two things shape poo: the tube and the time. Your digestive tract is one long, hollow, twisting tube. In the large intestine, water is pulled out of the leftover food, and as the water leaves, the waste gets harder and harder until it is solid.

gross.q: Why is poo brown?
gross.a: Poo is brown because of a dye your body makes. Your liver makes bile, a digestive juice that helps you digest fats, and your gallbladder squeezes it into your small intestine when you eat. Bile carries bilirubin, a yellowish substance your body makes when it breaks down old red blood cells.

gross.q: Why does poo smell?
gross.a: Poo smells because of gases made by bacteria. Your large intestine is home to enormous numbers of bacteria, and their job is to break down the bits of food your stomach and small intestine could not digest. As they work they make gases, and a few of those gases contain sulphur.

gross.q: Why is some poo green?
gross.a: The brown in poo is made right at the end of its journey. Bile carries bilirubin, a yellowish substance, and only when bacteria in the large intestine change bilirubin into stercobilin does the poo turn brown. Green poo is very common in babies.

gross.q: Why does sweetcorn come out looking the same as it went in?
gross.a: Only the outside of the sweetcorn comes out the same. Every kernel wears a tough coat, called the seed coat, made mostly of two plant fibres, hemicellulose and cellulose. Cellulose is what makes plant cell walls strong; wood and paper are mostly cellulose.

gross.q: Why do we need to poo every day?
gross.a: You do not have to, and many people do not. When scientists in Bristol asked nearly 1,900 people about their bowel habits, once a day was the most common pattern, but it was still a minority: only about 40 per cent of men and 33 per cent of women had a regular once-a-day rhythm. Doctors only start to call it constipation when someone poos fewer than three times a week, or the poo is hard, dry and difficult to pass.

gross.q: Why do we have snot?
gross.a: Snot is mucus, and your nose makes it on purpose. The thin, damp lining inside your nose produces it all day long. It has three jobs.

gross.q: Why is snot green when you have a cold?
gross.a: The green is not the germs. It is you fighting back. When a cold virus settles in your nose, your body sends in white blood cells to attack anything it does not recognise, and those cells travel out in your snot.

gross.q: Why do we get bogeys?
gross.a: A bogey is snot that has done its job and dried out. All day, the mucus in your nose catches dust, dirt, pollen and germs that come in with every breath. Tiny waving hairs called cilia push that loaded mucus towards the front of your nose.

gross.q: Why do people pick their nose?
gross.a: Because bogeys get in the way. When dried mucus builds up inside your nose it can make breathing feel blocked and uncomfortable, and picking is an instinctive way to clear it, done without thinking. Nearly everybody does it.

gross.q: Why do we sneeze?
gross.a: A sneeze is your nose's way of throwing something out. When the inside of your nose gets tickled or irritated, by dust, cold air, pepper, pollen or the swelling from a cold, nerves send a message to a spot in your brain stem that scientists call the sneeze centre. That centre runs a fixed programme.

gross.q: Why can you not sneeze with your eyes open?
gross.a: Because your eyelids are on the sneeze centre's list. A sneeze is a reflex, which means your brain stem runs it like a set recipe without asking you. That recipe includes a deep breath in, the head tipping back, the throat closing, the chest and belly muscles squeezing, and the eyes shutting.

gross.q: Why does pepper make us sneeze?
gross.a: Black pepper contains a chemical called piperine, and piperine is very good at setting off a tiny sensor in your nose. The nerves lining the inside of your nose carry sensors called TRP channels that detect things which sting or burn. One of them, TRPV1, is the same sensor that fires when you eat a hot chilli.

gross.q: Why does bright sunlight make some people sneeze?
gross.a: Nobody knows for certain, and that is the honest answer. About one person in four sneezes when they step out of a dark building into bright daylight. It even has a name: the photic sneeze reflex, and photic just means to do with light.

gross.q: Why do we make spit?
gross.a: Spit, or saliva, is made day and night by glands in your mouth: one pair in front of and just below your ears, one pair under your jaw, one pair under your tongue, and hundreds of tiny ones. They release about one to two litres a day. It is mostly water, but the other bits matter.

gross.q: Why does your mouth water when you smell food?
gross.a: Your body starts digesting food before any of it goes in. The thought, sight, smell or taste of something tasty tells your brain that a meal is coming, and the brain sends signals down the nerves to your salivary glands, which begin pumping out spit. Scientists call this the cephalic phase, meaning the head phase, and it gets your mouth ready to wet, taste and start breaking down the food.

gross.q: Why do we dribble when we sleep?
gross.a: Your mouth makes spit all day and all night. While you are awake you hardly notice, because you swallow it without thinking. Asleep, that changes.

gross.q: Why does spit go stringy when you are thirsty?
gross.a: Spit is mostly water. Mixed into it is a slippery substance called mucin, which your glands make to keep the inside of your mouth lubricated. When you are short of water, your glands make less spit.

gross.q: Why do we get a runny nose in the cold?
gross.a: Your nose is a heater. Its lining is packed with tiny blood vessels, and air passing over them is warmed before it goes on to your lungs. On a cold day the nose works harder: the blood vessels inside your nostrils open wider, bringing more warm blood to the surface to heat the icy air.

gross.q: Why do we cough?
gross.a: A cough is your body blasting something out of your airways: a bit of dust, a crumb that went the wrong way, or the extra mucus that comes with a cold. It happens in three quick stages. First you take a deep breath in.

gross.q: Why does phlegm come up when you are ill?
gross.a: Your airways are lined with a thin blanket of mucus all the time. It is sticky on purpose. Dust and germs you breathe in get trapped in it, and tiny hairs called cilia beat together to sweep the dirty mucus up and out of your lungs.

gross.q: Why do we hiccup?
gross.a: Under your lungs sits a big dome of muscle called the diaphragm. Every breath in, it pulls down; every breath out, it relaxes. A hiccup is that muscle giving a sudden, jerky tug it did not mean to give.

gross.q: Why does your nose whistle sometimes?
gross.a: Inside your nose, the two nostrils are separated by a thin wall called the septum. It is made of soft cartilage at the bottom, solid bone at the top, and skin on both sides. Ear, nose and throat doctors know one cause of a whistling nose well.

gross.q: Why do we get a blocked nose on one side at a time?
gross.a: Your nose takes turns. Inside each nostril is spongy tissue that can fill with blood and swell. At any moment one side is swollen and narrow while the other is open and doing most of the breathing.

gross.q: Why do we get scabs?
gross.a: When you scrape or cut your skin, your body needs to stop the bleeding and seal the wound straight away. Tiny bits in your blood called platelets rush to the spot and stick together like glue, trapping other blood cells and a thread-like protein called fibrin to make a plug across the gap. As this plug dries out on the surface, it hardens into a scab.

gross.q: Why is it hard not to pick a scab?
gross.a: Under a scab, your skin is busy at work. New skin cells are being made and broken blood vessels are being fixed, and skin that is healing can feel itchy. Fresh scars can be itchy too.

gross.q: Why do cuts bleed?
gross.a: Blood travels all around your body through a network of tubes called blood vessels, and the tiniest ones, called capillaries, run just under your skin. When you cut yourself, you tear through the skin and slice open some of these blood vessels, so blood escapes out through the gap instead of staying inside the pipes. Luckily your body has a repair crew ready.

gross.q: Why is blood red?
gross.a: Blood is made of a yellowish liquid called plasma, with red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets floating in it, and it is the red blood cells that give blood its colour. Each one is packed with a protein called haemoglobin, and haemoglobin's job is to carry oxygen around your body. When haemoglobin picks up oxygen in your lungs, it turns a bright red.

gross.q: Why do bruises change colour?
gross.a: A bruise starts when a knock breaks some of the tiny blood vessels under your skin. Blood leaks out of those vessels and pools in the tissue, and it is that trapped blood you can see through your skin, not a mark on the surface. At first a bruise usually looks red or purplish, because the leaked blood is still fairly fresh.

gross.q: Why do we get spots?
gross.a: Your skin is covered in tiny holes called pores, and most of them contain a gland that makes an oil called sebum to keep your skin and hair moisturised. During puberty, hormones make these glands produce extra sebum, and sometimes a pore gets clogged with too much oil, dead skin cells and ordinary bacteria that live on everyone's skin. A blocked, irritated pore is what shows up as a spot: it might be a whitehead, a small red bump, or a pustule with a white tip of pus.

gross.q: Why do we get blackheads?
gross.a: A blackhead is a clogged pore whose top has stayed open at the surface instead of closing over. Inside, oil called sebum has mixed with dead skin cells and plugged the pore. Even though the top is open to the air, it is not dirt that turns it dark.

gross.q: Why do we sweat?
gross.a: Your body works best at a steady temperature, close to 37 degrees Celsius, and a part of your brain called the hypothalamus keeps watch over it. When you get hot, from exercise or warm weather, the hypothalamus sends a message to sweat glands in your skin, telling them to get to work. They push a watery fluid called sweat out through tiny openings called pores.

gross.q: Why does sweat smell?
gross.a: Fresh sweat coming straight out of your skin has almost no smell at all; it is mostly just water. The smell appears afterwards, when bacteria that live naturally on everyone's skin start feeding on the sweat and other substances in it. As they break these down, the bacteria produce the smellier compounds that you notice, rather than the sweat itself ever being stinky.

gross.q: Why do feet smell?
