gross.a: Feet work hard, and shoes and socks trap them in a warm, damp, dark space, exactly the kind of place bacteria like best. These bacteria live on your feet all the time, and sweat gives them plenty to multiply in, especially if you go without socks. Once settled in, the bacteria feed on dead skin cells and oils from your skin, and as they do, they release waste as organic acids, and it is those acids that smell bad.

gross.q: Why do armpits smell more than arms?
gross.a: Sweat on its own barely smells at all. The difference is which glands make it. Your arms are covered in eccrine glands, which make a thin, watery sweat for cooling you down.

gross.q: Why do we get blisters?
gross.a: A blister is a small pocket of clear fluid that forms under a layer of skin. Most come from friction: something rubbing again and again in one spot, like a new shoe or a spade handle. The rubbing damages the skin, and fluid collects underneath to protect the sore patch while it heals.

gross.q: Why does skin peel after sunburn?
gross.a: Sunburn is not really a burn from heat. It is damage to the DNA inside your skin cells, caused by strong ultraviolet light from the sun. Your body treats those damaged cells as a problem to clear away.

gross.q: Why do fingers wrinkle in the bath?
gross.a: For a long time people thought wrinkly bath fingers were simply waterlogged skin, swollen up like a sponge. That is not quite it. Soaking washes the natural oil off your skin, letting water soak into its outer layer, but the wrinkling itself is switched on by your nervous system: tiny blood vessels in the fingertip narrow, pulling the surface into valleys.

gross.q: Why do we get goosebumps?
gross.a: Under every hair on your body sits a tiny muscle called the arrector pili. Goosebumps happen when those muscles suddenly contract, tugging the hair upright and pushing up a little bump of skin around it. Doctors call this the pilomotor reflex.

gross.q: Why do we get dandruff?
gross.a: Dandruff is not caused by dirty hair, and you cannot catch it from someone else. The flakes are bits of dead skin coming off the scalp. The exact cause is not known, but it is likely a mix of things: your scalp's own natural oil, called sebum, and a yeast called Malassezia that naturally lives on skin.

gross.q: Why do we get warts?
gross.a: Warts are small, firm bumps caused by a virus from the human papillomavirus family, usually called HPV for short. The virus gets into skin through a tiny cut, scratch or hangnail, which is why nail-biters are more wart-prone, and it can spread from touching another person's wart or a surface like a shower floor or towel. Once the virus is inside, it can take weeks or months to grow into the rough little bump you see and feel.

gross.q: Why does dead skin come off when you scrub?
gross.a: Your outer skin is not one fixed layer; it is a slow-moving conveyor belt. New cells form at the bottom of the epidermis, and over about two weeks to a month they travel upward, getting flatter and tougher as they go, until they die and reach the surface. What you see and touch on your hands is really a layer of dead cells, and they are always flaking off, whether you scrub or not: you lose roughly thirty to forty thousand of them every single minute.

gross.q: Why does a paper cut hurt so much?
gross.a: Nobody has studied paper cuts directly, but scientists have studied how well fingertips sense pain, and the answer is: unusually well. In tests, people could tell exactly where a small painful spot was far better on a fingertip than on the back of the hand. Oddly, that is not because fingertips are packed with extra pain-sensing nerve fibres.

gross.q: Why do we have earwax?
gross.a: Earwax is made by glands in the skin lining the outer part of your ear canal, and it has an important job. It keeps the skin there moist, so your ears do not get dry and itchy. It contains natural chemicals that help fight off infections that could otherwise hurt the delicate skin inside your ear canal.

gross.q: Why is earwax different colours?
gross.a: Earwax comes in two genetically determined types, and which one you have is written into your genes, just like eye colour. Dry earwax is brittle and flaky, and its colour ranges from pale to a brownish-grey. Wet earwax is darker, sticky and can look almost like honey.

gross.q: Why should you never put anything in your ear?
gross.a: Your ear canal and eardrum are delicate, and poking at them can hurt them, even if it does not feel sharp or sudden. Doctors say the same thing again and again: never put anything into your ear, not even a cotton bud or your own finger. Earwax usually clears itself, working slowly towards the opening on its own.

gross.q: Why do we get sleep in our eyes?
gross.a: While you are awake, blinking constantly washes a thin film of tears across your eyes, helping wash away germs and dust and keeping the surface moist. That film has three layers: a slippery mucus layer, a watery layer, and an oily layer on top. At night your eyelids stay shut and you stop blinking, but your eyes do not stop working.

gross.q: Why do eyes water when you cut onions?
gross.a: Cutting into an onion breaks open its cells, and that releases a chemical called a lachrymatory factor into the air. The moment it touches the surface of your eye, it stings, and your eyes react exactly the way they do to any irritant, like smoke or grit: they make extra tears to try to flush it away. Scientists have measured just how common this is.

gross.q: Why do we get eye bogeys when we are ill?
gross.a: When your eyes are fighting an infection, they make more of a sticky fluid called discharge than usual. Doctors call red, irritated eyes like this conjunctivitis, or pink eye, and it can be caused by a virus, by bacteria, or even by allergies such as hay fever. Whatever the cause, it can make the white of your eye red, itchy, gritty and watery.

gross.q: Why does breath smell in the morning?
gross.a: Bacteria live in your mouth all the time, mostly on your tongue, where tiny leftover bits of food and flakes of dead skin cells collect. While you are awake, talking, eating, drinking and swallowing keep washing this surface fairly clean. Overnight, none of that happens for hours on end, so the bacteria have all night to quietly break the trapped food and skin cells down, and that process makes smelly compounds.

gross.q: Why do teeth go yellow?
gross.a: The outer layer of your tooth, the enamel, is a hard, pale shield, and underneath it is dentine, which doctors describe as the yellow substance that makes up most of a tooth. Over time, two things can make teeth look more yellow. Certain foods and drinks, like tea, coffee and red wine, leave tiny coloured particles on the enamel surface, and these build up gradually if they are not brushed away.

gross.q: Why does plaque grow on teeth?
gross.a: Your mouth is home to huge numbers of bacteria, and that is completely normal. Plaque is what happens when those bacteria build a sticky home for themselves on your teeth. Every time you eat or drink something sugary, the bacteria feast on the sugar and multiply, clumping together into a soft, colourless film that clings to the enamel.

gross.q: Why do we lose our baby teeth?
gross.a: You start life with 20 baby teeth, and by about the age of five or six they begin to fall out one by one. Each baby tooth comes loose because a permanent tooth is growing in the jaw underneath it, and as that new tooth pushes upward it gradually shoves the old one out of its way. Losing baby teeth like this makes room for a full adult mouth: by around age twelve or thirteen, most people have all 32 permanent teeth in place, ready to last for the rest of their life.

gross.q: Why do gums bleed when you brush?
gross.a: Bleeding gums when you brush are usually the first sign of mild gum inflammation called gingivitis, and it happens because of plaque. Plaque is an invisible, sticky layer of germs that forms on your teeth and gums every day, and it contains bacteria that irritate the gum tissue if it is not cleaned away. Irritated gums swell slightly and become more delicate, so even gentle brushing or flossing can make tiny blood vessels near the surface bleed a little.

gross.q: Why does a wobbly tooth bleed?
gross.a: A tooth on its way out is not just held less firmly, the gum around it changes too. As a baby tooth loosens, the tissue and tiny fibres holding it in place gradually break down, and the gum nearby often becomes a little inflamed; doctors describe the areas around a wobbly tooth as places of localised gum inflammation. Inflamed gum tissue is thinner and more delicate than healthy gum, so its tiny blood vessels sit closer to the surface and bleed more easily when the tooth is wiggled, brushed, or bumped.

gross.q: Why do we have a tongue that can taste gross things?
gross.a: Your tongue is covered in bumps called papillae, and tucked inside them are around 10,000 taste buds that can pick out sweet, sour, bitter and salty flavours. Tasting things is not just about enjoying food, it is also a built-in warning system. Bitter tastes in particular are often linked to substances that could be harmful or poisonous, so when something tastes strongly bitter or "off," your brain treats that as a signal to be careful and can make you want to spit it straight out.

gross.q: Why does your tongue go white sometimes?
gross.a: A pale, whitish coating on your tongue is usually nothing more than a normal build-up called tongue coating. It forms from a mix of tiny dead skin cells that flake off your tongue's surface, leftover bits of food, and ordinary mouth bacteria, all held together in a thin layer across the bumpy papillae. Saliva usually washes this away while you are awake and eating, but your mouth makes far less saliva overnight, so the coating often builds up while you sleep and is at its thickest first thing in the morning.

gross.q: Why do we get hairs in our nose?
gross.a: The hairs just inside your nostrils are called vibrissae, and they act like a doorstep filter for the air you breathe in. As air rushes past, these stiff little hairs catch bigger bits of dust, pollen and other floating particles before they can travel further inside. Anything that gets past the hairs meets a sticky layer of mucus further inside the nose, plus even tinier hairs that keep sweeping the trapped debris along and out of the way.

gross.q: Why do we get nits?
gross.a: Nits are the eggs of head lice, tiny insects about the size of a sesame seed that live in human hair and feed on small amounts of blood from the scalp. Once lice settle into someone's hair, they start laying nits, gluing each egg firmly to a strand of hair close to the scalp where it is warm. Head lice cannot jump or fly, so they spread mainly through head-to-head contact, or by sharing things like hats, combs, brushes and hairbands that an infested person has used.

gross.q: Why does hair go greasy?
gross.a: Almost every hair on your head grows out of a tiny tube called a follicle, and attached to nearly every follicle is a sebaceous gland that makes oil. This oil, called sebum, spreads along the hair shaft and normally does a good job of keeping hair shiny and a little bit waterproof. During puberty, though, the body produces much higher levels of hormones called androgens, and these hormones tell the sebaceous glands to work harder and pump out extra sebum.

gross.q: Why do belly buttons collect fluff?
gross.a: Belly button fluff, or navel lint, mostly comes from tiny fibres of your shirt, and body hair is what carries it there. Fine hairs on the tummy usually point towards the belly button, and their surface is covered in microscopic scales that all face the same way, like overlapping roof tiles. Every breath makes your shirt shift very slightly against your skin, and that tiny movement drags loose fibres along the hairs, always in the direction the scales allow: towards the navel.

gross.q: Why do dung beetles roll poo?
gross.a: Dung beetles roll balls of animal poo so they can carry food away from a crowded dung pile, where rivals steal, and bury it somewhere safer. Fresh droppings are scarce and competition is fierce, so roller species quickly sculpt a ball and push it off in a straight line. Once buried, the ball becomes a private meal and, for many species, a nursery: the female lays an egg in it so the growing grub has a ready food store.

gross.q: Why do flies vomit on their food?
gross.a: Flies do not chew. Most of the flies that land on your picnic have mouthparts shaped like a spongy straw, so solid food is useless until it turns into liquid. When a hungry fly settles, it releases enzyme-rich saliva, and often regurgitated fluid from a storage pouch called the crop, onto the surface.

gross.q: Why do maggots appear on old meat?
gross.a: Maggots do not appear from nowhere. Adult female flies lay tiny pale eggs on moist decaying meat, manure or other rotting organic matter. In warm weather the eggs can hatch in roughly eight to twenty hours into soft, legless larvae people call maggots.

gross.q: Why do slugs make slime?
gross.a: Slugs make slime because they need a moving, sticky track and a damp coat for life on land. Special glands in the foot release mucus that acts as both a lubricant and an adhesive, letting the soft body glide while still gripping vertical surfaces. The same slime forms a barrier that slows water loss, which matters because slugs dry out easily.

gross.q: Why do worms come out when it rains?
gross.a: Worms do not surface after rain simply to escape drowning. Earthworms breathe through moist skin and can survive for days underwater, so flooded burrows alone do not explain the pavement parade. Scientists think wet weather lets them travel farther across the surface than they could push through soil, because they must stay damp.

gross.q: Why do mosquitoes drink blood?
gross.a: Only female mosquitoes drink blood, and they do it for eggs, not for everyday energy. Both sexes sip flower nectar and plant juices for sugar fuel, but most females cannot mature a batch of eggs without a blood meal. Proteins and iron in vertebrate blood supply the building blocks for egg development.

gross.q: Why do mosquito bites itch?
gross.a: A mosquito bite itches because of the saliva she injects while feeding, not because of the tiny hole itself. As blood is drawn up one channel of the proboscis, saliva travels down another. That saliva carries proteins that stop clotting and help the meal flow, and your immune system treats those proteins as invaders.

gross.q: Why do head lice love clean hair?
gross.a: Head lice do not specially love clean hair, and they do not prefer dirty hair either. They are parasites that cling to hair shafts and feed on blood from the scalp, so washing habits make little difference to them. Getting lice is not a sign of poor hygiene; anyone can catch them through head-to-head contact, which is common when children play close together.

gross.q: Why do spiders eat their webs?
gross.a: Many orb-weaving spiders eat their old webs to recycle costly silk. Spider silk is made of protein, and spinning a fresh trap uses up stores the spider cannot afford to waste if prey is scarce. Before rebuilding, often daily, the spider gathers the used threads, digests them, and sends the recovered materials back to the silk glands for the next web.

gross.q: Why do cockroaches survive almost anything?
gross.a: Cockroaches seem to survive almost anything because they combine tough bodies, flexible diets and slow cell division with rapid breeding, not because they are magic. They recycle decaying matter, taste carefully, and some can go weeks without food. Their cells divide mainly around moulting, so radiation damages them less than it damages constantly dividing human cells; tests show they can endure doses many times higher than a lethal human dose, though flour beetles beat them.

gross.q: Why do bees vomit to make honey?
gross.a: Bees do not vomit honey from a true stomach. Foragers suck nectar into a special crop called the honey stomach, separate from the gut that digests food for the bee herself. Enzymes in that crop begin breaking complex sugars down while the bee flies home.

gross.q: Why do ants carry their dead?
gross.a: Ants carry dead nestmates out of the nest to keep the colony clean and lower the chance that microbes will spread. Workers detect chemical changes on a corpse: in some species fatty acids such as oleic acid build up after death, while in others life-signalling chemicals fade within about an hour. Either cue marks the body as something to remove.

gross.q: Why do fleas jump so high?
gross.a: Fleas jump so high because they store energy in a springy pad of the rubber-like protein resilin, then release it in a sudden catapult. Ordinary muscle alone cannot launch a millimetre-scale insect that fast. High-speed films show the force travels through leg levers to the feet, so the flea pushes off with its toes rather than its knees.

gross.q: Why do ticks swell up?
gross.a: Ticks swell because they drink a huge blood meal and their bodies are built to stretch around it. After finding a host by sensing breath, heat and movement, a tick cuts into the skin, inserts barbed mouthparts, and often glues itself in place with a cement-like saliva. Soft ticks may feed quickly, but many hard ticks stay attached for days, sucking blood while pumping saliva that can numb the spot.

gross.q: Why do stink bugs stink?
gross.a: Stink bugs stink on purpose. Adults and young carry scent glands on the underside of the thorax and along the abdomen. When a bug is disturbed, handled or crushed, it releases strong-smelling defensive chemicals from those glands.

gross.q: Why do bombardier beetles fire hot spray from their bottoms?
gross.a: Bombardier beetles fire hot spray from their bottoms by mixing two stored chemicals only at the last moment. One sac holds hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinones; a tough rear chamber holds enzymes. When threatened, the beetle squeezes the stored fluid into that chamber.

gross.q: Why do caterpillars turn to mush inside a chrysalis?
gross.a: Inside a chrysalis a caterpillar largely digests itself so it can rebuild as a butterfly or moth. Hormonal signals start histolysis: enzymes dissolve most larval tissues into a protein-rich soup. If you opened a chrysalis at the wrong moment, that liquid would spill out.

gross.q: Why do woodlice curl into a ball?
gross.a: Some woodlice, often called pill bugs, curl into a tight ball when poked or shaken. The behaviour, called conglobation, tucks soft legs and underside inside overlapping armour plates so predators meet a hard sphere instead of a soft belly. The ball can also help the animal roll into leaf litter and disappear.

gross.q: Why do dust mites live in your bed?
gross.a: Dust mites live in your bed because mattresses and pillows are warm, slightly damp and packed with their favourite food: tiny flakes of shed human skin. These microscopic relatives of spiders thrive in ordinary homes no matter how tidy you are. They prefer humid rooms and gather in bedding, carpets and soft furnishings where skin scales collect.

gross.q: Why do dogs eat poo?
gross.a: Some dogs eat poo, a habit called coprophagy, and scientists still debate exactly why. Surveys of thousands of pet dogs found that about one in six often eats dog stools, usually ones that are less than two days old. The dogs were not worse at toilet training than others, and diet alone did not explain it, though greedy eaters did it more.

gross.q: Why do dogs sniff each other's bottoms?
gross.a: When dogs meet, they often put their noses right under each other's tails. That is not rude in dog language. It is how they read a chemical greeting.

gross.q: Why do cats cough up furballs?
gross.a: Cats are careful groomers. Their tongues are covered with tiny backward-pointing spikes called papillae that comb loose hair toward the throat. Much of that hair is made of tough keratin, which a cat cannot digest.

gross.q: Why do rabbits eat their own droppings?
gross.a: Rabbits do not eat ordinary hard pellets for fun. They make a second kind of soft dropping called a cecotrope. Food first travels through the gut, then tiny plant fibres are sent into a large pouch called the caecum.

gross.q: Why do vultures have bald heads?
gross.a: A bare head looks odd, but it helps a vulture in more than one way. San Diego Zoo explains that featherless skin keeps feathers from getting tangled and filthy when the bird pushes into a carcass, and sunlight on bare skin may help clean it. University of Glasgow research adds another job: thermoregulation.

gross.q: Why do vultures wee on their own legs?
gross.a: New World vultures sometimes let wee and droppings run down their bare legs. The behaviour is called urohidrosis. San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance explains that as the liquid evaporates it cools the bird, like sweat cooling you, which helps on very hot days.

gross.q: Why do hagfish make slime?
gross.a: Hagfish look soft and helpless, yet they carry a famous defence. Along their sides sit many slime glands. When attacked, they jet a thick precursor into the water.

gross.q: Why do skunks spray?
gross.a: Skunks spray as a last-chance defence, not because they are always angry. Special glands near the base of the tail hold a yellowish, oily musk rich in sulphur chemicals called thiols, which smell like onion or rotten egg. The US National Park Service says a striped skunk can aim a stream at a face about ten to fifteen feet away, and stores only about two ounces, enough for a few shots before needing days to refill.

gross.q: Why do hippos fling their poo?
gross.a: Hippos do not just drop dung and walk away. While they poo, they wag a short, strong tail so hard that faeces and wee spray in a wide shower. San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance fact sheets call this ritualized dung-showering.

gross.q: Why do owls cough up pellets?
gross.a: Owls often swallow mice, voles, and small birds whole. Soft meat is digested, but bones, teeth, fur, and feathers cannot break down safely. Inside the muscular gizzard, those hard leftovers are packed into an oval mass.

gross.q: Why do penguins poo in stripes?
gross.a: Parent chinstrap and Adélie penguins must guard eggs and chicks, so they cannot stroll far to toilet. Instead they shuffle to the nest rim, point their bottoms outward, lift the tail, and fire a jet of semi-liquid poo. The stream can travel about forty centimetres, leaving a pale or pink stripe that points away from the nest.

gross.q: Why do sloths only poo once a week?
gross.a: Sloths live in slow motion. Smithsonian's National Zoo notes their metabolism is only about forty to forty-five percent of what you would expect for their size, and food can sit in the gut for roughly a month. Because digestion is so slow, faeces and urine are usually passed only about once a week, often at the same base of a favourite tree.

gross.q: Why do camels spit?
gross.a: Camel "spit" is not ordinary saliva. San Diego Zoo explains that an upset camel brings up stomach contents mixed with spit and projects the mess to surprise or bother whatever feels threatening. Cheeks bulge first as a clear warning.

gross.q: Why do frogs eat their own skin?
gross.a: Frogs and toads regularly shed the outer layer of their skin. Mucus loosens the old sheet, which often tears down the back; the animal then pulls it off with its limbs and frequently swallows it. This skin-eating is called dermatophagy.

gross.q: Why do sharks have such stinky breath?
gross.a: Sharks do not breathe out lung air the way you do; they pull oxygen from water through gills. What people call "stinky shark breath" is mostly chemistry and leftovers. Shark flesh holds high levels of urea, a salt-balancing chemical also linked to wee.

gross.q: Why do whales have poo that floats?
gross.a: Whale poo often leaves the body as a loose, cloudy plume rather than a heavy pellet. Because whales must surface to breathe, much of that waste is released near the top of the ocean, and the flocculent plume tends to stay where sunlight can reach. PLOS ONE researchers called this upward recycling the "whale pump": mammals carry nutrients eaten in deeper water back toward the sunlit layer as faecal plumes.

gross.q: Why do baby koalas eat their mum's poo?
gross.a: Joey koalas begin life on milk inside the pouch. Eucalyptus leaves are tough and toxic to most animals, so a joey is not born ready to digest them. San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance explains that mothers later produce a special soft material called pap, rich in the microbes a joey needs to handle eucalyptus.

gross.q: Why do sea cucumbers throw out their insides?
gross.a: Soft sea cucumbers cannot dash away from crabs or fish, so some use a startling defence. When threatened, they may eject internal organs through the rear end, a process called evisceration. NOAA Fisheries notes California sea cucumbers can expel organs to deter predators and then regrow them.

gross.q: Why do elephants poo so much in one day?
gross.a: Elephants are enormous plant-eaters. San Diego Zoo reports its elephants may eat one hundred twenty-five pounds or more of food daily and each deposit about three hundred pounds of poo, much of that weight coming from the huge volumes of water they drink. Wild adults can produce up to about one hundred fifty kilograms of nutrient-rich dung in a day, according to University of California research highlighting how that waste feeds dung beetles and savanna life.

gross.q: Why does milk go off?
gross.a: Milk goes off because tiny microbes grow in it and change its chemistry. Even after pasteurisation, some bacteria can get in again, or hardy ones that like the cold can slowly multiply in the fridge. As they feed on milk sugar, called lactose, they make acids that sour the taste and make the liquid thicken and separate.

gross.q: Why does cheese stink?
gross.a: Cheese gets its smell from living microbes that cheese-makers put to work on purpose. Bacteria, yeasts and moulds break down milk sugar, protein and fat as the cheese ages. Their leftovers include volatile molecules, especially sulphur compounds and ammonia, that float into the air and hit your nose.

gross.q: Why does blue cheese have mould in it on purpose?
gross.a: Blue cheese is made with a special mould, often Penicillium roqueforti, that cheese-makers add on purpose. They pierce the young cheese with needles so air can reach the inside, letting the mould grow in blue-green veins. That mould breaks down fats and proteins, creating the creamy texture near the veins and the sharp, tangy flavour blue cheese is known for.

gross.q: Why does bread go mouldy?
gross.a: Fresh bread from a hot oven is free of living mould, but the air is full of invisible mould spores. After baking, during cooling, slicing or wrapping, those spores can settle on the loaf. Bread is moist and only mildly acidic, which moulds love, so the spores sprout into fuzzy colonies of Rhizopus, Penicillium or Aspergillus.

gross.q: Why does fruit go soft and brown?
gross.a: Softening and browning are two related changes. As fruit ripens, a plant gas called ethylene helps enzymes loosen the cell walls, so apples, bananas and similar fruits turn softer and sweeter. Browning happens when cells are cut, bruised or over-ripe and membranes break.

gross.q: Why do eggs smell of rotten eggs when they go bad?
gross.a: That famous rotten-egg smell is a gas called hydrogen sulfide. When eggs spoil, bacteria such as Proteus can grow inside after getting through the shell or being helped by cracks and warm storage. Those microbes break down sulphur-rich proteins in the white and yolk and release hydrogen sulfide into the air.

gross.q: Why does fish smell fishy?
gross.a: Truly fresh fish smells faintly of the sea or a clean lake, not strongly fishy. Ocean fish keep a chemical called trimethylamine oxide, or TMAO, inside their cells to balance salty seawater. After the fish dies, bacteria and natural enzymes convert TMAO into trimethylamine, or TMA, and that is the classic fishy smell.

gross.q: Why do onions make you cry?
gross.a: Onions pack sulphur chemicals in their cells as a defence. When you cut an onion, you smash those cells and mix an enzyme called alliinase with sulphur compounds, making sulfenic acids. In onions, a second enzyme called lachrymatory-factor synthase quickly rearranges one of those acids into a gas named syn-propanethial S-oxide.

gross.q: Why does garlic make your breath smell?
gross.a: Crushing garlic releases sulphur compounds that create its bold flavour. In your mouth and gut those chemicals are changed into several smelly gases. Some fade quickly, but one called allyl methyl sulfide lasts much longer.

gross.q: Why does asparagus make wee smell?
gross.a: Asparagus contains a special sulphur compound called asparagusic acid. When your body digests it, the acid breaks into several small, smelly sulphur gases, including methanethiol and dimethyl sulfide. Those gases leave your body in wee and evaporate into the air as soon as the warm liquid hits the toilet, which is why the smell arrives quickly after a meal.

gross.q: Why does beetroot make wee pink?
gross.a: Beetroot is packed with red-purple pigments called betacyanins, including betanin. After you eat beetroot, some of those pigments can pass through your gut unchanged and leave your body in wee, turning it pink or even deep red. This harmless colouring is called beeturia.

gross.q: Why does chewing gum not digest?
gross.a: Chewing gum is mostly a soft, rubbery base plus sugar or sweeteners and flavour. Your digestive enzymes can break down the sweeteners and some flavour oils, but they cannot digest the gum base. Food rules even describe that base as a nonnutritive masticatory substance made of natural or synthetic elastomers, resins and softeners.

gross.q: Why do we vomit when we eat something bad?
gross.a: Vomiting is your body's emergency eject button for the stomach. When you eat something contaminated, sensors in the gut and a special brain area that watches the blood detect toxins, germs or irritation. Nerves carry the alarm to a coordinating region in the brainstem.

gross.q: Why does vomit look like that?
gross.a: Vomit is mostly whatever was in your stomach, mixed with strong stomach juices. Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid, so fresh vomit is usually very acidic and can burn a little at the back of the throat. You may see half-chewed food if you have eaten recently, or a thinner liquid if the stomach was emptier.

gross.q: Why does the fridge smell?
gross.a: A fridge smells when volatile gases from food escape into the cold air and hang around. Even at low temperatures, microbes and enzymes slowly break proteins, fats and sugars into small smelly molecules such as amines, ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, aldehydes and alcohols. Those gases mix, stick to plastic shelves and can soak into nearby soft foods, so last week's leftover onions can perfume this week's custard.

gross.q: Why does honey never go off?
gross.a: Honey lasts so long because microbes find it almost impossible to grow there. It is packed with sugars and holds very little free water, so its water activity often sits around 0.5 to 0.6, below what most bacteria and moulds need. The high sugar also pulls water out of any wandering microbe by osmosis.

gross.q: Why do we get food poisoning?
gross.a: Food poisoning happens when you eat or drink something that carries harmful germs or the toxins they make. Bacteria such as Campylobacter, Salmonella and E. coli, and viruses such as norovirus, are common causes.

gross.q: Why does yoghurt have bacteria in it on purpose?
gross.a: Yoghurt is milk that helpful bacteria have transformed on purpose. Makers add starter cultures, usually Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus delbrueckii subspecies bulgaricus. Those bacteria eat lactose and produce lactic acid.

gross.q: Why do some people eat insects?
gross.a: People in many parts of the world eat insects because they are nutritious and have long been part of traditional meals. About two billion people include them in their diets. Edible insects can provide high-quality protein, healthy fats, fibre and minerals such as iron and zinc.

gross.q: Why do we have germs living inside us?
gross.a: Your body is home to trillions of tiny living things called microbes. Most of them are friendly helpers, not enemies. In your gut they break down leftover bits of food your own enzymes cannot finish, and they help make useful vitamins such as vitamin K.

gross.q: Why does your tummy rumble?
gross.a: That rumbling has a proper name: borborygmus. It happens when muscles in your stomach and small intestine squeeze in waves called peristalsis. Those waves push food, liquid and gas along your digestive tube, a bit like squeezing toothpaste from a tube.

gross.q: Why does your tummy gurgle after you eat?
gross.a: After a meal your digestive tract becomes especially busy. Stomach and intestine muscles mix food with digestive juices and push the mixture onward. Air you swallowed while eating, plus gas made as bacteria work on leftovers, get shuffled about at the same time.

gross.q: Why do we get diarrhoea?
gross.a: Diarrhoea means your poo is loose and watery. A common reason is a bowel infection called gastroenteritis, often started by a virus such as norovirus or rotavirus, and sometimes by bacteria or parasites from contaminated food or water. When the gut is irritated, contents can move too quickly, or the large intestine cannot soak up enough water from the stool.

gross.q: Why do we get constipated?
gross.a: Constipation means poo becomes hard, dry and difficult to pass, or you go much less often than usual. It often happens when stool stays too long in the large intestine. The colon keeps absorbing water, so the leftover waste grows firmer.

gross.q: Why is wee yellow?
gross.a: Wee gets its sunny colour from a pigment called urobilin (also known as urochrome). When old red blood cells are broken down, the body makes a yellow-orange substance called bilirubin. Gut bacteria help turn bilirubin into urobilinogen.

gross.q: Why does wee smell stronger some days?
gross.a: Fresh wee is mostly water mixed with waste the kidneys have filtered out. When you drink enough, that waste is well diluted and the smell stays mild. On days when you have had less to drink, sweated a lot, or first thing after a long sleep, the kidneys hold on to water.

gross.q: Why do we need to wee more when it is cold?
gross.a: In chilly weather your body protects its warm core. Blood vessels in your skin and fingers tighten, which pushes more blood toward the centre of your body. That shift can raise pressure in the central blood volume.

gross.q: Why do we get a temperature when we are ill?
gross.a: A raised temperature, or fever, is often your body's clever defence, not the illness itself. When germs invade, immune cells release chemical messengers. Those signals tell a control centre in the brain called the hypothalamus to turn the body's thermostat up.

gross.q: Why do we shiver with a fever?
gross.a: Shivering with a fever feels odd because you may already be warmer than usual, yet you feel cold. Here is why. When the hypothalamus raises the temperature set point, your actual body heat is still below that new target.

gross.q: Why does pus form?
gross.a: Pus is a thick, pale fluid that gathers where your immune system is fighting, often at an infected spot. White blood cells called neutrophils rush from the blood to attack invading bacteria or other germs. As they battle, some of those cells die, along with bits of damaged tissue and the germs themselves.

gross.q: Why do we get tonsil stones?
gross.a: Tonsil stones, or tonsilloliths, are little pale lumps that form in the pits of your tonsils. Tonsils sit at the back of the throat and have deep folds called crypts. Bits of food, dead cells, saliva and bacteria can settle in those crypts.

gross.q: Why does our appendix exist if it can burst?
gross.a: The appendix is a small finger-shaped pouch on the large intestine. For years people thought it did nothing useful, but research now suggests it has helpful jobs. It holds lots of immune tissue that helps train defences in the gut.

gross.q: Why does the stomach not digest itself?
gross.a: Your stomach makes strong acid and a protein-cutting enzyme called pepsin to mash food into a liquid pulp. Those chemicals could harm living tissue, yet the stomach wall usually stays safe. Special surface cells pour out a thick coat of mucus that blankets the lining.

gross.q: Why do we sweat when we are sick?
gross.a: Sweating when you are ill often means the fever is changing, not that sweat is chasing germs away. While a fever is rising, the brain's set point is high, so you may feel cold and shiver to gain heat. Later, when infection signals fade or fever medicine works, the hypothalamus lowers the set point back toward normal.

gross.q: Why do we feel sick on a boat?
gross.a: Seasickness is a kind of motion sickness. Your brain judges movement by combining messages from your eyes, inner ears, muscles and joints. On a rocking boat your inner ears feel the up-and-down and side-to-side motion, but if you stare at a cabin wall or a book, your eyes may report that the world is still.

gross.q: Why does the body make so much mucus?
gross.a: Mucus is the slippery gel that lines your nose, airways, mouth, stomach, intestines and even the surface of your eyes. Your body makes it all the time, not only when you have a cold. It keeps delicate tissues moist so they do not dry out, and it acts like flypaper for dust, pollen and germs you breathe in.

gross.q: Why is the gut as long as a bus?
gross.a: Your intestines need a huge amount of surface to soak up nutrients, so they are coiled tightly inside your belly. Stretch an adult's small intestine end to end and Nemours KidsHealth says it measures about 22 feet (about 6.7 metres), plus roughly 5 feet (about 1.5 metres) of large intestine. That total of around eight metres is why people sometimes picture the gut as roughly the length of a short bus.
